strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and timely problem: making transformer-based autoregressive models competitive for 3D molecule generation, where diffusion models currently dominate.

The overall system design is coherent and well-motivated: canonical tokenization via inertial frames plus RDKit-based canonical ordering addresses SE(3) and permutation symmetry, GeoRoPE injects geometric inductive bias into standard attention, and the hierarchical factorization (discrete atom type via cross-entropy, continuous coordinates via diffusion loss, Li et al., 2024a) cleanly handles the hybrid token structure.

The empirical results on the standard QM9 and GEOM-Drugs benchmarks are strong: InertialAR achieves the best Atom Stability (99.3%/87.2%) and Molecule Stability (94.7%) among all compared diffusion and AR baselines, against a broad set of recent methods (EDM, GeoLDM, MiDi, UniGEM, Geo2Seq).

The proposed class-conditional generation setting with functional-group-based Molecule Class IDs and the Hit Rate metric is an interesting new evaluation direction, and the CFG-based molecule editing demonstration (Figure 3) is a compelling capability.
The appendix includes a formal treatment (Theorem 1/2) of why a fourth anchor node is needed to uniquely fix inertial frame axis directions, with a proof by contradiction.

Evaluation extends beyond the saturated small-molecule benchmarks to a much larger and more diverse dataset (B3LYP/PubChemQC, 1M molecules), where baselines degrade significantly but InertialAR maintains high validity.
weaknesses: No ablation studies are provided anywhere in the manuscript. The individual contributions of the inertial-frame canonicalization, canonical reordering, RoPE-3D, and the Nyström distance encoding are never disentangled. Claims such as 'merely using RoPE-3D cannot learn adequate information' and 'direct regression yields poor performance' are stated as empirical findings without any supporting numbers.

Reproducibility is weak: there are no implementation details (model size, number of layers, diffusion loss hyperparameters, number of denoising steps, training compute, sampling budget), no code release, and the appendix contains only background material and proofs rather than experimental details.

The central theoretical treatment is inconsistent and under-specified: Theorem 1 (main text) requires the fourth point to be NOT on the y-z or x-z plane, while Theorem 2 (appendix) states it must be 'coplanar with the three basis vectors'. More importantly, the degenerate-eigenvalue case (symmetric molecules, acknowledged in Section 3.1) is not actually resolved: within a degenerate eigenspace the canonical frame is not unique, so the same molecule can map to different token sequences. The claim that such frames are 'physically equivalent' does not address the resulting training-sequence ambiguity.

The theoretical analysis ignores chirality: a right-handed inertial frame canonicalization can map mirror-image (enantiomeric) structures to related canonical poses, and the paper never discusses whether the model is chirality-aware, which is chemically important.

The headline claim of 'state-of-the-art on 7 of 10 metrics' is technically accurate but overstates the picture: on QM9, InertialAR is NOT best on Validity (97.4 vs. MiDi 97.9) or Valid&Uni (92.5 vs. MiDi 97.0), and on GEOM-Drugs it is not best on Validity (96.8 vs. GeoLDM 99.3). It wins 3 of 6 unconditional metrics on QM9/GEOM.

The B3LYP comparison uses only two baselines (EDM, Geo2Seq) on a self-selected 1M subset of a new dataset, and Geo2Seq collapses catastrophically (2.7% Valid&Uni), raising concerns about baseline tuning/adaptation on this new benchmark. The absolute Molecule Stability (24.2%) remains low despite being presented as a success.

The paper motivates AR models by computational efficiency and flexible variable-length generation versus diffusion, but never reports sampling time or cost. Since each atom's coordinates are generated via an iterative diffusion denoising process, the claimed efficiency advantage over diffusion models is unverified.

The conditional-generation benchmark is self-constructed (functional-group SMARTS matching), and baselines are compared without evidence they were given equal opportunity to condition; CFG scale and hyperparameter selection for each method are not reported.

Presentation is rough in places: Equation (15) contains a duplicated factor, the main text and appendix substantially duplicate preliminary material (Sections 2 vs. A.2/A.3), the proof in Appendix D is informal in steps, and there is no limitations discussion.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely question: whether autoregressive Transformers can serve as a competitive generative paradigm for 3D molecule generation, and the engineering combination (inertial-frame tokenization + GeoRoPE + hierarchical AR with diffusion loss) is coherent and clearly motivated.

Empirical results are strong on the headline metrics: best Atom Stability and Molecule Stability on QM9 (99.3%/94.7%) and best Atom Stability on GEOM-Drugs (87.2%), and the new large-scale B3LYP evaluation is a welcome addition beyond the standard QM9/GEOM-Drugs benchmarks.

The introduction of a class-conditional generation task with functional-group-based Molecule Class IDs and a Hit Rate metric is a useful new evaluation protocol, and the reported conditional results (83.3% average hit rate) are substantially better than the compared baselines.

TheNyström-based pairwise-distance encoding is an interesting attempt to inject RBF distance information into a standard Transformer attention score while retaining compatibility with LLM-style architectures.
The appendices provide detailed derivations for the fourth-node frame disambiguation and the Nyström construction, which aids understanding of the method.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the individual components are largely assembled from prior work — inertial-frame/PCA canonicalization (Guo et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025a; Cheng et al., 2025a), RoPE extended to 3D coordinates, Diffusion Loss directly adopted from Li et al. (2024a), and hierarchical AR for molecules (Cheng et al., 2025b). The paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond this combination.

Chemical soundness of the canonical tokenization is not adequately analyzed. Aligning to the principal axis frame cannot distinguish enantiomers, so mirror-image (chiral) molecules plausibly collapse to the same canonical sequence — a significant issue for molecular generation that is never discussed. Additionally, for near-degenerate inertia eigenvalues (symmetric or near-symmetric molecules) the eigenvectors are numerically unstable, and the claim that 'all valid frames are physically equivalent' hand-waves a real discontinuity in the tokenization; the perturbation-based tie-breaking of RDKit canonical ranking may also be unstable, effectively injecting label noise into the AR supervision.

Overclaimed and inconsistently reported SOTA results. The abstract claims SOTA on '7 of the 10 metrics', while the contributions say 3 of 6 on QM9/GEOM-Drugs. In Table 1, MiDi clearly outperforms InertialAR on QM9 Valid&Uni (97.0 vs 92.5), and uniqueness is never reported separately, hiding a possible ~5% duplicate rate. The selective framing of which metrics count is misleading.

Inefficient inference undermines the central motivation. The paper motivates AR over diffusion by avoiding 'computationally intensive iterative sampling', yet coordinate prediction uses iterative diffusion denoising for every single atom, so sampling complexity scales as O(n × diffusion steps) with a sequential dependence on n atoms. No sampling-time or cost comparison against diffusion baselines is provided to support the efficiency claim.

Incomplete baselines and potentially unfair comparisons. On B3LYP only EDM and Geo2Seq are compared; Geo2Seq's near-total collapse (2.7% Valid&Uni) is suspicious and may reflect inadequate adaptation to a 50-atom-type vocabulary rather than method inferiority. Stronger recent baselines (UniGEM, MiDi) are absent from the B3LYP and conditional tables. For conditional generation, EDM was not designed for functional-group conditioning and CFG tuning details for baselines are not given, making the large hit-rate gaps hard to interpret.

Missing ablations and reproducibility details. There are no ablations isolating the contributions of canonical reordering, RoPE-3D vs. Nyström encoding vs. both, diffusion loss vs. regression, or the choice of m anchors and RBF bandwidth σ. Model sizes, training hyperparameters, compute budgets, number of runs, and variance/error bars are not reported, and no code release is mentioned.

Technical and presentation errors. Theorem 1 (main text) requires the fourth node 'not on the y-z plane or x-z plane', while Theorem 2 (appendix) states it 'is coplanar with the three basis vectors' — the two statements are contradictory, and the proof's matrix in Eq. (34) contains an evident typo (k2k3 appearing twice in the off-diagonal). Equation (15) writes p(ai+1|hi) = p(ai+1|hi) · p(ci+1|ti+1, hi), which is dimensionally inconsistent as stated. Figure 2's caption contradicts the text about which quadrant x4 occupies.
Limitations are not discussed: there is no limitations section addressing chirality, degenerate frames, generation order sensitivity, or the per-atom diffusion cost.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important problem: adapting autoregressive transformers to 3D molecule generation requires solving both canonical tokenization (SE(3) + permutation invariance) and hybrid discrete/continuous next-token prediction. The proposed combination of inertial-frame canonicalization, GeoRoPE, and a hierarchical type-then-coordinates factorization with diffusion loss is a coherent and well-motivated design.

The inertial frame axis-direction ambiguity is handled with a fourth anchor point, and the underlying geometric idea (three points cannot fix a rigid frame; four non-coplanar points can) is clearly illustrated and mostly convincing at an intuitive level.

The Nyström-based injection of pairwise distance information into a standard transformer attention score (Eq. 14) is a neat trick that preserves LLM-compatible architecture while making attention geometry-aware; the derivation in Section C is self-contained.

Experimental coverage is broad: QM9, GEOM-Drugs, a large-scale B3LYP benchmark, and a new class-conditional generation/molecule-editing task with a Hit Rate metric. InertialAR is competitive or state-of-the-art on most reported metrics (e.g., 99.3% AtomSta and 94.7% MolSta on QM9; large gains on conditional hit rate 83.3% vs. 25.7%/42.2%).

The conditional-generation task (functional-group Molecule Class IDs via SMARTS) is a practically relevant formulation, and the CFG-based molecule editing demonstration (Figure 3) is an interesting capability.
weaknesses: Theorem statements are inconsistent and the proof is sloppy, which undermines confidence in the theoretical contribution. Theorem 1 (p.4) requires the fourth point to be 'not on the y-z plane or x-z plane,' whereas the surrounding text and Figure 2 require x4 to lie in the first quadrant of the x-y plane. More seriously, Theorem 2 (Appendix D) states the fourth point must be 'coplanar with the three basis vectors' while the proof explicitly assumes it is 'nonplanar' — the stated theorem appears to be wrong as written. The contradiction argument in Eqs. (33)-(34) also contains errors (the displayed 2x2(2Q Q^T - I) matrix is malformed, and the step concluding Q_{f,0} = cv from the given expression does not follow).

The well-known brittleness of inertial-frame canonicalization is not addressed: near-degenerate inertia eigenvalues (asymmetric yet near-symmetric molecules, which are ubiquitous in drug-like data) cause the canonical pose to change discontinuously under tiny coordinate perturbations, and the treatment of exactly symmetric molecules (CO2, CH4) is acknowledged as ambiguous but its effect on AR training is never quantified.

No ablation studies are reported. The claim that 'merely using RoPE-3D cannot learn adequate information, while explicitly adding the pairwise information is more informative' is an empirical assertion with no supporting table; contributions of GeoRoPE vs. Nyström encoding vs. the fourth-node disambiguation vs. hierarchical factorization are not separated.

Comparisons are incomplete and potentially unfair on the flagship large-scale result: B3LYP is benchmarked against only EDM and Geo2Seq, and Geo2Seq collapses to near-zero (2.7% Valid&Uni, 0.0% MolSta), which suggests possible baseline misconfiguration rather than a meaningful comparison. MiDi and UniGEM are absent from B3LYP and from several QM9/GEOM-Drugs metrics.

The motivating claim that AR models are more efficient than diffusion models is not substantiated: the per-token diffusion loss requires iterative denoising at inference for every atom, so sampling cost may be substantial. No sampling speed, wall-clock, or step-count comparison to diffusion baselines is provided.

Reproducibility is weak: no code release, no model sizes, parameter counts, training hyperparameters, denoising-step counts, or CFG scales are reported; single-run results with no variance or significance analysis.

Large portions of the appendix (Sections E and F: positional encoding survey, complex numbers, quaternions, rotations) are textbook-level tutorial material that displaces space that should have gone to implementation details, ablations, or limitations.

The conditional-generation setup is fully self-constructed (Molecule Class IDs, Hit Rate metric, and baseline retraining), so the large hit-rate gaps over EDM/Geo2Seq cannot be externally validated, and failure modes (e.g., hit rates on rare classes, mode collapse under high guidance) are not analyzed. The paper also lacks a limitations discussion.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies the two key obstacles (SE(3)- and permutation-invariant tokenization; hybrid discrete-continuous tokens) for autoregressive 3D molecule generation and addresses each with a concrete mechanism (inertial-frame canonical tokenization, GeoPE, hierarchical AR with Diffusion Loss).

Strong empirical results across three benchmarks: SOTA on 4/6 metrics for QM9 and GEOM-Drugs (Table 1) and on all 4 metrics for the large-scale B3LYP dataset (Table 2), plus a new class-conditional generation task with functional-group labels where InertialAR attains much higher hit rates (avg. 83.3%) than EDM and Geo2Seq (Table 3).

Honest treatment of theoretical limitations of inertial-frame canonicalization: the paper acknowledges degenerate eigenvalues and axis-flip discontinuities (citing Dym et al. 2024), quantifies their empirical rarity (Tables 4-5), provides a formal theorem and proof for the fourth-node sign disambiguation (Appendix D), and explicitly disclaims claiming a theoretically perfect canonicalization.
Useful ablations: Diffusion Loss vs. L2 regression (dramatic collapse with L2, Table 6) and removal of canonical atom ordering (Table 7), supporting the two central design decisions.

Extends RoPE-style relative positional reasoning (ManhattanPE) and uses Nyström low-rank RBF features (EuclideanPE) in a clean way that stays compatible with standard Transformer attention, with a complete derivation in Appendix C.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the main components (Diffusion Loss from Li et al. 2024a, RoPE-inspired PE from Su 2021, Nyström approximation, PCA/inertial-frame canonicalization, RDKit canonical ordering, classifier-free guidance) are all existing techniques; the contribution is primarily their combination and engineering, which reduces the conceptual advance relative to the strong empirical claims.

Missing comparison to the closest autoregressive competitor: the paper cites Cheng et al. (2025b) 'Scalable autoregressive 3D molecule generation' even borrowing the hierarchical AR design rationale from it, yet never compares against it empirically on any benchmark, weakening the SOTA claim within the AR paradigm.

Baseline coverage is thin on the new B3LYP dataset and in the conditional setting: only EDM and Geo2Seq are compared. Geo2Seq's near-total collapse on B3LYP (2.7% Valid&Uni) is surprising and raises concerns about baseline tuning/fairness; without more baselines (e.g., GeoLDM, UniGEM) it is hard to judge whether the large-scale gains are real or protocol artifacts.

The claim of AR efficiency over diffusion is asserted but never substantiated: no sampling-time, throughput, or parameter-count comparisons are reported anywhere, despite efficiency being a core motivation in the introduction.

Robustness analysis is incomplete: stability is measured only for the farthest-atom anchor identity, but swaps in eigenvalue ordering (near-degenerate principal moments) could also cause discontinuities; moreover, all robustness statistics are computed on training datasets, and behavior on the model's own generated (potentially more symmetric or degenerate) structures is not analyzed.

The Hit Rate metric for controllable generation is self-defined by the authors; no orthogonal validation (e.g., property distributions, energy plausibility, or downstream usefulness of edited molecules in Figure 4) is provided, and CFG editing results are only qualitative.

Reproducibility details are sparse in the manuscript as presented: no model sizes, training configurations, sampling settings (number of denoising steps), or compute budgets are given in the main text or the reviewed appendices; the code link is promised but the paper's own experimental spec is insufficient to independently reproduce headline numbers.

Some design choices are empirically motivated rather than justified: e.g., the claim that explicitly adding Euclidean distance information 'is more informative' is stated from observation without ablation isolating ManhattanPE vs. EuclideanPE contributions.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated problem: adapting autoregressive Transformers to 3D molecule generation requires both an SE(3)- and permutation-invariant tokenization and a mechanism for hybrid discrete-continuous tokens. The proposed decomposition (canonical inertial frame + deterministic reordering + hierarchical AR with Diffusion Loss) is sensible and clearly presented.

The empirical robustness analysis of the inertial frame (Appendix E.1: principal-moment degeneracy frequency, farthest-atom flip rates under coordinate perturbations) is unusually thorough and honest, and the authors explicitly disclaim that they are not proposing a theoretically perfect canonicalization. The limitation discussion around Dym et al. (2024) discontinuity results is appropriate.

Results on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs are competitive with or better than strong diffusion baselines (e.g., best MolSta 94.5 on QM9, best AtomSta 87.0 on GEOM-Drugs), and ablations on Diffusion Loss vs. L2 regression (Table 6) and canonical indexing (Table 7) are informative.
The Nyström-based EuclideanPE derivation (Appendix C) that makes pairwise-distance information compatible with standard Transformer attention is a nice engineering contribution.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated. The paper claims to be 'the first work that turns inertial-frame canonicalization into a generation-ready tokenization' for AR 3D generation, but Geo2Seq (Li et al., 2024b), the closest baseline, already performs canonicalization-based tokenization for Transformer AR molecule generation, and Cheng et al. (2025b) on scalable AR 3D generation is cited only briefly. The delta over these works appears to be substituting PCA/inertial frames for their canonicalization and adding GeoPE — an incremental combination rather than a fundamentally new paradigm.

The core motivation for AR over diffusion is 'highly efficient and flexible generation,' yet the paper reports no sampling speed, wall-clock time, number of function evaluations, or model parameter counts anywhere. The central efficiency claim is left entirely unsupported, while coordinate generation still requires iterative diffusion denoising per atom, undermining the argument that AR avoids 'computationally intensive iterative sampling.'

Baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns. On B3LYP, only EDM and Geo2Seq are compared, and Geo2Seq catastrophically collapses (2.7% Valid&Uni), which suggests possible suboptimal tuning or preprocessing mismatch rather than a genuine capability gap; no effort is made to diagnose this. UniGEM and GeoLDM — which beat InertialAR on some QM9/GEOM-Drugs metrics — are absent from the B3LYP and conditional settings.

The class-conditional generation study is on a self-constructed benchmark (Molecule Class IDs via SMARTS matching on QM9) with a self-introduced metric (Hit Rate), compared only against EDM and Geo2Seq. Establishing 'state-of-the-art across all 5 metrics' on a benchmark the authors themselves define, with baselines that were not designed for this objective, weakens the significance of that claim.

Ablations are incomplete relative to the design space: the two GeoPE components (ManhattanPE and EuclideanPE) are never ablated individually or jointly, so the contribution of each — and of GeoPE at all relative to simpler 3D positional encodings — is not established. ManhattanPE is largely a 3D extension of 2D RoPE (Su, 2021), making component-level evidence important.

The sign-disambiguation anchor (fourth node = farthest atom off the x-y plane) introduces a discrete selection whose instability under perturbation, while shown to be rare on QM9/Drugs, is a discontinuity in the tokenization map; generated molecules near such boundaries could receive inconsistent canonical frames at inference, and this failure mode is analyzed only for the training data, not for generated samples.

Reproducibility details are thin in the main text: model size, training compute, Diffusion Loss hyperparameters (denoising steps, σ schedule), anchor count m for Nyström, and guidance-scale values are not reported in the provided manuscript, and the code link is truncated. Without these, the strong headline numbers are hard to independently verify.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies the two core obstacles (SE(3) invariance and permutation invariance of tokenization, plus hybrid discrete/continuous token prediction) for autoregressive 3D molecule generation and addresses each with a concrete mechanism (inertial-frame canonicalization + RDKit canonical reordering, GeoPE, hierarchical type/coordinate prediction with Diffusion Loss).

The GeoPE design is technically sound: the derivation that ManhattanPE makes attention scores relative-position-dependent (Eqs. 5-7), and the Nyström-based EuclideanPE that allows pairwise RBF distances to be recovered via inner products (Appendix C), are carefully constructed and well explained.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: state-of-the-art or near-SOTA results on QM9 and GEOM-Drugs, a new large-scale B3LYYP evaluation, a new class-conditional generation setting with a functional-group labeling pipeline and Hit Rate metric, and CFG-based molecule editing — a breadth beyond typical papers in this area.

Honest and thorough treatment of the known theoretical weakness of PCA/inertial-frame canonicalization: the paper cites the frame-averaging literature (Puny et al., Dym et al.), provides a formal proof for the fourth-node sign disambiguation (Appendix D), and quantifies empirically that degeneracy and sign flips are rare on the datasets used (Appendix E.1).
Useful ablations isolating each component: Diffusion Loss vs. L2 regression (dramatic collapse for L2), canonical indexing on/off, and robustness analyses.
Code is stated to be available, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central canonicalization mechanism is known to be theoretically fragile — discontinuous and non-unique under degenerate principal moments (which the paper itself acknowledges via Dym et al. 2024). The robustness analysis (Appendix E.1) is performed only on training datasets; the more relevant question is how often the AR model generates near-degenerate or symmetric molecules at inference, where frame instability could cause train/test distribution mismatch. This is not analyzed.

Novelty is largely system-level integration rather than new methodology: inertial-frame canonicalization, canonical SMILES ordering (RDKit), diffusion loss (Li et al. 2024a), hierarchical AR heads, and CFG are all existing techniques. The paper's claim of being 'the first work that turns inertial-frame canonicalization into a generation-ready tokenization' is defensible, but the margin over concurrent atom-based AR tokenization work (e.g., Cheng et al. 2025b, Lu et al. 2025b) is not clearly delineated.

Evaluation concerns: (i) the standard validity/stability metrics are known to be imperfect proxies for molecular quality, and the large MolSta gains come from very low baselines; (ii) on B3LYP only two baselines are compared, and Geo2Seq's near-total failure (2.7% Valid&Uni) is surprising and under-explained — this could indicate an evaluation-protocol mismatch rather than a genuine gap; (iii) no model size, training cost, or sampling speed comparison is reported, despite the introduction motivating AR over diffusion by computational efficiency — AR next-token generation with per-token diffusion sampling is often not faster in practice.

The class-conditional benchmark, class labels, and Hit Rate metric are all newly constructed by the authors, with baselines limited to EDM and Geo2Seq; results on a self-defined benchmark are less convincing than results on established community benchmarks.
Inconsistency between ablation configuration and headline results is acknowledged but not quantified, making it harder to cross-reference ablation numbers with Table 1.
Chirality and stereochemistry are not discussed: canonical SMILES ordering without stereochemical markers may conflate enantiomers, which matters for drug-like molecule generation.
